### Why it Matters
This release prioritizes AI-driven workflows by integrating dedicated neural accelerators into the GPU, marking a significant shift in Apple's desktop hardware strategy. While general users may see minimal daily performance gains, the increased memory bandwidth and display capabilities provide a necessary upgrade for professionals working with high-refresh monitors and local large language models.

articles.title: OPPO is putting three 200MP cameras on its next flagship phone
articles.author: techkritiko@gmail.com (Jay Bonggolto) , Jay Bonggolto
articles.content:
What you need to know
- The OPPO Find X10 Pro Max will feature three 200MP rear sensors, making it the first phone with a setup like this.
- OPPO is once again working with Hasselblad to push the phone’s imaging capabilities further.
- The 200MP main camera reportedly combines an f/1.5 aperture, CIPA 6.5-level stabilization, and DeepPix tech for better challenging-light performance.
OPPO's Find X10 Pro Max is set to launch in China this month, and the company has just confirmed that it’ll come with what could be the most absurd camera array we’ve ever seen on a smartphone. The headline? Not one, not two, but three 200MP sensors around the back. Yes, you read that correctly.
OPPO's Find series product lead, Zhuo Shijie, didn't mince words on Weibo either, calling this the "most powerful" (machine translated) device in its class this year. That’s a bold statement, but the hardware might actually live up to it.
Apparently, this is the world’s first triple 200MP camera system, developed in partnership with Hasselblad, again. The main shooter is rumored to use Samsung’s new ISOCELL HPC sensor (1/1.3-inch) and comes with an f/1.5 aperture, CIPA 6.5-level stabilization, and new DeepPix tech that pushes dynamic range to 17EV. This means it could handle tricky lighting much better than typical high-res sensors.
Perhaps the bigger flex here is the 200MP ultrawide. This is the first time a sensor this big has been slapped on an ultrawide. You get a 124-degree field of view and f/2.2 aperture, with OPPO claiming 102% more light captured versus the last generation.
The 200MP periscope telephoto is also no slouch, with a 70mm focal length, f/2.1 aperture, and CIPA 7.5 stabilization, which is better than the main camera. It also does a 10cm telephoto macro.
All three lenses are tipped to shoot in 8K for videos, and it’s apparently the only phone that supports full-focal-length 8K Log capture.
The OPPO Find X10 series is expected to launch with ColorOS 17 based on Android 17 around September 17. There are also rumors of a Dimensity 9600 Pro chip, a 6.78-inch 2K LTPO OLED with 144 Hz refresh, and a massive 8,000mAh battery.

Meanwhile, the standard Find X10 will presumably get dual 200MP cameras, so the Pro Max is clearly the one for photography obsessives.

articles.title: Trezor Supply Chain Breach Now Impacts 81,000 Customers
articles.author: Phil Muncaster
articles.content:
Cryptocurrency wallet manufacturer Trezor has revealed that a breach at a key shipping partner has affected 67,000 more customers than originally thought.
In an update posted on September 4, the hardware specialist said it was informed that the trove stolen from ShipMonk also included order data from the time period November 2019 – August 2021.
When the original breach notification was posted on August 13, the firm claimed that only data from between May 10 and August 8 2026 was involved.
The new victim count represents a 479% increase on the original estimate.
Full details were exposed in the incident, including customer names, emails, phone numbers, shipping addresses and order numbers.
“Be aware of the increased risk of phishing,” the firm warned. “The leaked information could be used for scam emails, fraudulent calls or letters, and could potentially expose affected individuals to physical security risks.”
Trezor customers have been a popular target for threat actors over the years. In 2022, it was forced to clarify that an email sent to customers warning of a major data breach at the firm was a scam designed to trick them into handing over their wallet recovery codes.
A Supply Chain Snafu
Trezor laid the blame for the recent breach firmly at the feet of its logistics partner, claiming that its data minimization policy wasn’t followed.
“Throughout our entire relationship with ShipMonk, we repeatedly requested and received written assurance confirming the deletion of the data, in line with our contract, data policy, and past communications,” it wrote in a post on X (formerly Twitter). “We are very disappointed that, despite receiving this confirmation, the data was not deleted in their systems.”
Trezor said it was still deciding whether to take legal action against the firm.
“We are in direct contact with ShipMonk to establish exactly what happened and which data was reached. ShipMonk has secured the affected systems and hardened its security after the incident,” it continued.
“We are also speeding up work on anonymous delivery in our shop, so that in the future less personal data has to leave our systems at all, and in the meantime you can already keep what you share to a minimum by using a PO box, parcel locker, or pickup point.”
articles.summary:
Hardware wallet manufacturer Trezor confirmed that a data breach at its shipping partner, ShipMonk, exposed the personal information of 67,000 additional customers, significantly exceeding initial incident estimates.

### Key Points
- The breach exposed names, email addresses, phone numbers, shipping addresses, and order details for customers between November 2019 and August 2021.
- The updated victim count represents a 479% increase over the 14,000 individuals originally reported by the company on August 13.
- Trezor stated that ShipMonk failed to delete customer data as required by their contract and data minimization policies.
- The company is currently evaluating potential legal action against the logistics provider following the security failure.
- Trezor is accelerating plans for anonymous delivery options and advises customers to use parcel lockers or PO boxes to protect their privacy.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the significant security risks posed by third-party logistics providers when handling sensitive customer data. It serves as a reminder that even companies with strong internal security can be compromised through supply chain vulnerabilities, potentially exposing users to targeted phishing and physical security threats.

articles.title: Oil Nears $100 as Markets Assess Fed Rate Expectations and Iran Tensions: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street Futures

articles.content:
© Dries Buytaert
U.S. stock futures were mixed on Tuesday as investors returned from the Labor Day holiday and assessed higher oil prices, rising bond yields, upcoming economic data and expectations for the Federal Reserve’s September policy meeting.
Developments in the Middle East also remained in focus, while markets continued to assess a stronger-than-expected August U.S. employment report.
Dow Jones Futures fell 0.8% to 53,013 points, while S&P 500 Futures declined 0.3% to 7,691.3 points. Nasdaq 100 Futures were unchanged at 29,593 points.
The moves followed the August employment report, which came in above expectations and prompted investors to reassess the outlook for U.S. interest rates.
Higher oil prices have also added another factor to the inflation outlook as markets consider the potential implications for Federal Reserve policy.
Investors are awaiting the weekly ADP Employment Change report, which uses a four-week moving average of private-sector employment to provide an additional measure of U.S. labour-market conditions.
The U.S. Treasury is also scheduled to auction three-year notes. Demand at the auction will provide an indication of investor appetite for U.S. government debt.
The auction comes after selling pressure in global bond markets pushed government borrowing costs higher. Bond prices and yields move inversely, meaning declining bond prices are accompanied by rising yields.
U.S. national debt has surpassed $40 trillion. The government issues Treasury securities to finance spending and refinance existing obligations, with higher yields increasing its borrowing costs.
Treasury yields also influence borrowing costs elsewhere in the economy, including mortgages and corporate debt, and are one of the factors investors use when valuing equities.
President Donald Trump on Monday called for an immediate end to Bombardier (TSX:BBD.B) sales in the United States.
Bombardier also trades in the U.S. as BDRAF. According to the supplied material, the U.S. accounts for more than half of the Canadian aircraft manufacturer’s revenue.
The company is expected to generate approximately $10.2 billion in revenue in 2026. Based on the geographic exposure cited in the supplied information, more than half of that amount would represent approximately $5 billion or more in annual U.S.-related revenue.
The supplied information does not identify a specific policy measure implementing Trump’s statement. Any eventual financial effect on Bombardier would depend on whether restrictions are introduced and their scope.
Geopolitical tensions remained elevated after Iran threatened to respond to what it described as U.S. “economic warfare” by establishing a maritime exclusion zone across the Persian Gulf.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said Iran had issued a warning through its latest missile attacks and that additional economic pressure would be met with an exclusion zone extending across the Gulf towards the perimeter of the U.S. blockade.
Rezaei also said Iran’s approach towards U.S. warships and military bases had been “fundamentally recalibrated.”
Attacks by Iranian-backed Houthi forces on Saudi Arabia have separately increased market attention on energy infrastructure and shipping routes in the region.
The Persian Gulf is an important route for global energy supplies. Disruption to shipping could affect oil availability and prices, although the scale and duration of any impact would depend on developments in the region.
Brent crude advanced 1.4% on Tuesday to a six-week high, marking a third consecutive session of gains.
The benchmark has recently traded near $99 a barrel as markets assessed U.S.-Iran tensions and the potential for further disruption to regional energy supplies.
A sustained increase in crude prices could contribute to higher transportation and production costs and affect inflation. The eventual implications for monetary policy would depend on the duration of higher energy prices, broader inflation data and the Federal Reserve’s assessment of economic conditions.
Markets are consequently monitoring whether Brent reaches or exceeds $100 a barrel alongside developments in bond markets, U.S. economic data and the Middle East.

articles.title: NBA 2K27 gives DLSS 5 a more faithful-looking game debut than feared, provided it’s running on the LeBron of GPUs
articles.author: James Archer
articles.content:
Bit of an anticlimax, really. After months of (justified) revulsion and anti-anticipation over Nvidia DLSS 5’s AI rendering, it’s now available in a live game - license laden b-baller NBA 2K27 - and it looks... maybe not that bad?
This not-that-badness does come at an enormous cost to performance, and I’m still sceptical of how DLSS 5 will handle something more stylised than 2K27’s devotedly realistic depictions of varnished court floors and face-scanned athletes. But given how artistically botching and/or ridden with rendering errors the earlier previews have been, this specific implementation, in this specific game, is at least inoffensive in the looks department.
Since DLSS 5 only currently has official support on RTX 50 series graphics cards, I tried it on two: an RTX 5080 at 1440p and an RTX 5050 at 1080p, both on top of Ultra settings with ray traced reflections and Quality-level DLSS upscaling enabled. And on both setups, it’s hard to argue that DLSS 5 slobbers filterslop all over NBA 2K27’s original artistic intent.
It probably helps, to stress the point, when the intention is already photorealism, the same goal that Nvidia explicitly identify as DLSS 5’s raison d'etre. Your brain likely expects 2K27’s players to resemble their real-life counterparts, in a similar way to how it wouldn’t expect Resident Evil Requiem to look like it was posted by a blue-ticked X user with the caption "Hollywood is finished lol". As such, when DLSS 5 rocks up and makes their skin slightly sweatier or their vests slightly more textured, it doesn’t look wrong. It doesn’t even 'look like AI', to my eyes - even in motion, there’s none of the artificial, overly glossy smoothness typical of fully genAI visuals.
Crucially, there are few signs of the excess detailing and outright errors that were evident in pre-release material, outside of some unnecessary eye-darkening. Facial structures appear unchanged - there’s no evidence DLSS 5 ever did literally reshape character model geometry, but its combination of visual changes did produce a facelift effect in certain promo shots - and darker skin tones aren’t uncomfortably lightened. The original reveal also included a warping football that suggested DLSS 5 would have frame gen-style problems rendering fast-moving objects, but the ball in the hands of a sprinting 2K27 dunksman remains steadfastly spherical. As well as it can with upscaling and motion blur, anyway.
Zoomed out with the default game cam, it even becomes hard to tell where DLSS 5 is having an effect and where it isn’t; I suspect developers Visual Concepts have simply made use of its masking feature to apply neural rendering to objects selectively, as opposed to essentially whacking a filter over the entire image. Either way, it’s a not-unpleasant surprise to see DLSS 5 still looking like a game here, rather than an AI-generated approximation of one.
Whether that stays true in other games - those that don’t share NBA 2K27’s love of photorealism – remains to be seen. DLSS 5 sidesteps many of the ethical problems with genAI: its machinations take place on your GPU, instead of an earthslaying data centre, and it functions as a glorified upscaler for existing art, rather than pretending to be original art itself. Yet because its model isn’t trained on a per-game basis, I don’t think it’s unfair to be worried about its potential to give supporting games a samey, unified look, much like the averaged-out tone of generated AI text, or how AI videos tend to have a certain giveaway sheen. Nvidia have said much about preserving artistic intent, and DLSS 5’s inclusion of dev-side masking and intensity adjustment tools are worth noting, but we won’t have a full idea of how flexible and faithful it can be until it expands beyond one sports sim.
DLSS 5 also has a more immediate drawback: performance. My RTX 5080 lost 54% of its 2K27 framerate at 1440p: an average 211fps dropped to 98fps with a single flick of the neural rendering toggle. With the diminishing returns of ultra-high framerates, that may not be ruinous in practice. The RTX 5050, however, took a sound thrashing at 1080p. 137fps with Ultra settings and ray tracing, a fine showing even with help from Quality-level upscaling, plummeted to 44fps with DLSS 5 enabled - a 67% performance tax. And as reassuring as it is to see the tech’s visuals showing some restraint, you can’t really say it looks 67% nicer.
NBA 2K27 has DLSS 4’s Multi-Frame Generation to make up the difference, though this genuinely is too much AI, too fast. While MFG objectively gets the numbers up, 3x mode averaging 99fps on the RTX 5050 (and 6x mode reaching 135fps), it still hurls back in your face all the same vexations that frame generation has produced since DLSS 3. 3x mode was enough to distort details - you can see the bending player ID tag and the ball thrower’s disintegrating hand in the screenshot below - while 6x added nastily edge distortions and ghosting effects. Considering the whole point of DLSS 5 is to make games look more realistic, MFG evidently isn’t the answer to its frame hunger, and that’s even before getting into frame gen’s added input lag.
I’m told that Nvidia are actively working to improve DLSS 5 performance on 50 series cards, after which they’ll switch focus to RTX 40 series support. That’s fine, though for all the grossness of that original reveal, and all the subsequent charm offensives about respecting intent, and all the resurging RTX On memes, it’s almost funny that NBA 2K27’s launch version of DLSS 5 is basically just the equivalent of path tracing with extra machine learning: a noticeable, if benign and selective graphical upgrade that’s just too demanding to be within reach of most PCs.
All the same, it could have been so, so much worse. I generally detest generative AI and the world it’s creating, where I can’t even trust that a freelance pitch in my inbox has been written by a living human. But I also believe in being a factually accurate hater, and factually, a DLSS 5-ified BA 2K27 still looks like NBA 2K27, mainly just with extra pores and perspiration. A decent start, aesthetically, even if it still has much to prove in future implementations.

articles.summary:
Nvidia has officially launched its DLSS 5 AI rendering technology in the game NBA 2K27, offering improved visual fidelity for photorealistic graphics at the cost of significant performance.

### Key Points
- Nvidia DLSS 5 is currently exclusive to RTX 50 series graphics cards, with future support planned for RTX 40 series hardware.
- Testing on an RTX 5080 showed a 54% drop in framerate, while an RTX 5050 experienced a 67% performance decrease at 1080p.
- The technology utilizes developer-side masking to selectively apply neural rendering, avoiding the "AI-generated" look seen in earlier, controversial previews.
- NBA 2K27 includes Multi-Frame Generation (MFG) to offset performance losses, though this feature introduces visual artifacts like ghosting and edge distortion.
- Unlike some generative AI tools, DLSS 5 processes data locally on the GPU rather than relying on external data centers.

### Why it Matters
The debut of DLSS 5 demonstrates that Nvidia can implement neural rendering without compromising a game's original artistic intent, provided the title focuses on photorealism. However, the substantial performance tax and hardware exclusivity suggest the technology remains in an early, demanding stage that may not yet be viable for mainstream PC gaming.

articles.title: North Korea-linked Hackers Hide a Backdoor Inside HAProxy
articles.author: Pierluigi Paganini
articles.content:
North Korean-linked hackers found a genuinely clever hiding spot for their malware: inside the actual source code of HAProxy, the load balancing software running at the edge of two South Korean companies’ networks. Rapid7’s research documents a previously undocumented Linux toolkit hitting South Korea’s automotive and media sectors, and the depth of integration here goes well beyond a typical backdoor bolted onto a system.
“A new Linux toolkit, identified by Rapid7 Labs, has been targeting organizations across South Korea’s automotive and media industries with minimal detection. The campaign made use of a HAProxy instance named “ted backdoor”, alongside trojanized versions of crond, agetty, atd, sshd, and polkitd.” reads the report published by Rapid7. “This previously undocumented framework enabled threat actors to execute remote commands on compromised servers, inject malicious scripts into web traffic, perform credential harvesting, and engage in long-term surveillance.”
The implant, which Rapid7 calls the “ted backdoor” based on debug strings the attackers left behind, isn’t a separate process running alongside HAProxy. It’s compiled directly into HAProxy’s own source code as a custom plugin, using the software’s native filter API, internal memory management, and event scheduler to intercept HTTP traffic while completely legitimate load balancing keeps running normally on top of it.
“The standout feature of this toolkit is its depth of integration with the target environment. The ted backdoor is compiled as part of the victim’s existing HAProxy version 2.8.12.” continues the report. “It uses its native filter API, internal memory pools, event scheduler, and process management infrastructure to intercept traffic and hide from monitoring, while genuine load balancing traffic operates as expected.”
Rapid7 explains, which is really the whole thesis of why this backdoor is so hard to spot: it’s not an addition to the software, it’s woven into it.
The backdoor receives commands through a surprisingly simple trick. The attackers send a request for a fake image at /favorite_list_2x_m500_ico.jpg. This switches the HAProxy filter into command-and-control mode.
The malware then saves the command in a named pipe and removes traces of the request from HAProxy’s internal counters. It also clears the forwarding buffers, so the request never reaches the backend server. The command ends at the load balancer, leaving nothing in the application logs to show that it happened.
This ability to erase its own traces makes the backdoor very different from a normal web shell. The C2 requests never reach the backend server and are also removed from HAProxy’s statistics.
As a result, neither the application logs nor HAProxy’s connection logs show that the attack happened. A security team checking the logs could find nothing suspicious because the backdoor has already erased the evidence.
Beyond remote command execution, the backdoor can quietly inject malicious scripts or entirely swap out page content for specific victims matched by IP address, browser fingerprint, or even a hidden authentication credential smuggled inside the Accept-Language header, effectively turning a company’s own load balancer into a watering hole against its own visitors. It also hooks response bodies carefully enough to hide the size difference caused by injected content, stripping the header that would let a browser notice the byte-range mismatch. That’s a level of protocol-level care that suggests real HAProxy internals expertise, not a quick copy-paste job.
The main backdoor also comes with a separate toolkit that modifies common Linux system daemons such as crond, agetty, atd, and sshd. These programs continue to work normally but also carry malicious features.
One component acts as an SSH keylogger. It captures passwords that administrators enter in plain text and quietly records them. Another tool, called curlRAT, contacts a remote server every 12 hours by default, or every 30 seconds when the attacker enables its fast-poll mode.
curlRAT also checks whether the system runs inside a virtual machine. If it does not find the expected signs, it refuses to run. This behavior suggests the attackers designed the malware to avoid sandboxes and other analysis environments.
Attribution here sits at medium confidence, and Rapid7 is upfront about the limits of what the evidence actually shows. The targeting pattern, simple XOR-based encryption, a custom substitution cipher, and command-server infrastructure already linked to APT37 by other threat intelligence feeds all point toward North Korean state involvement, with some technical overlap also drawing comparisons to a concurrent Lazarus Group campaign against South Korean media sites.
“Further evidence is necessary to make a more definitive assessment. Moreover, the presence of ngx_* prefixed routines within the ted backdoor suggest code reused from an nginx backdoor. The ngx_* prefixed routines were observed during the latest Funnull campaign, where (similar to our case) a custom nginx filter was registered to hook HTTP traffic, and simple XOR encryption was applied to the configuration file.” Rapid7 states. “However, other than a similar naming convention, no significant code-level overlaps exist to support a stronger linkage.”
If your organization runs HAProxy, or really any edge component handling SSL termination and traffic routing, the practical lesson here is uncomfortable but simple: that software deserves the same scrutiny as your actual application servers, not less. The Hacker News confirmed in early September that the specific command domains used in this campaign have already gone dark, returning no DNS records at all, which is useful for reviewing historical logs but does nothing to stop whatever comes next from the same operators. Checking a load balancer’s own logs isn’t enough anymore when the backdoor’s entire design goal is making sure those logs never see it in the first place.
“ted backdoor and curlRAT were designed to persist during long-term espionage operations with the ability to steal cookie sessions, credentials, redirect selected users, conduct drive-by download attacks, and hide evidence of the tampered page to a specific range of IPs to evade detection.” concludes the report. “Defenders should treat any edge component managing user traffic, SSL, or runtime modules with the same strict security standards as their main application servers. Relying on the component’s own logs is not enough; securing these systems requires independent network correlation, memory behavioral analysis, and binary integrity checks.”
Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon
(SecurityAffairs – hacking, North Korea)
articles.summary:
North Korean-linked hackers are compromising South Korean automotive and media firms by embedding a sophisticated "ted backdoor" directly into the source code of HAProxy load balancing software.

### Key Points
- Researchers at Rapid7 identified a Linux toolkit that integrates malicious code into HAProxy version 2.8.12 using its native filter API.
- The backdoor intercepts HTTP traffic and executes remote commands by triggering a hidden mode via requests for a specific fake image file.
- Malicious activity is erased from internal logs and statistics, allowing the malware to perform credential harvesting and surveillance without leaving a trace.
- The campaign also deploys trojanized versions of standard Linux daemons, including crond, agetty, and sshd, to maintain persistence and log administrator passwords.
- Evidence, including infrastructure and encryption methods, suggests the involvement of North Korean state-sponsored actors, potentially linked to APT37 or the Lazarus Group.

### Why it Matters
This attack demonstrates a shift toward deep-level infrastructure compromise where malicious code is woven into essential network components rather than running as separate processes. Organizations must now implement independent binary integrity checks and memory behavioral analysis, as relying on standard application logs is no longer sufficient to detect sophisticated edge-based threats.

articles.title: ‘Smart TV That Spies on You Even When It’s Off’ Is My #1 Christmas Gift Item

‘Smart TV That Spies on You Even When It’s Off’ Is My #1 Christmas Gift Item
We all knew our smart TVs were using absolutely any data they could collect on us for the sake of ads, but this is a new level of creepy.
Photo via Unsplash, Glenn Carstens-Peters Splinter Privacy
If you know me, then surely you’d attest to how I’m always saying aloud how I wish more data could be collected by the digital devices in my vicinity in order to further personalize the attempts I encounter on every digital screen to extract more money from my bank account. It’s just that I crave efficiency in all things; why should I have to inform advertisers that a beloved pet has passed away before they start throwing ads for tiny tombstones at me? It would be far easier if even more devices in my vicinity could just listen in 24/7 instead, so they’d have a better chance of deciphering what I’m crying about and intuit what they could sell me to directly address it. And until now, I’ve always suffered the annoyance of assuming that if my smart TV happens to be turned off, it can’t simultaneously gather data about my e-commerce habits. Thankfully, it seems LG smart TVs may have delivered what I’ve been craving all along: A smart TV that goes out of its way to spy on the user even when it’s off. Finally, a way to surrender the last shreds of my privacy!
That allegation comes per a new investigation this week from a YouTube channel of all places, in conjunction with Level1Techs and a team of independent security researchers. In a more than two-hour video uploaded to the channel Gamers Nexus, the combined team lays out evidence demonstrating how various LG smart TV models store and utilize user data, even when the TV is currently off. Simultaneously, the investigation claims to have uncovered various security weaknesses that could allow hackers or bad actors to seize control of these already privacy-invading “features,” allowing for data collection on users by hackers in addition to TV manufacturers. Such security concerns have supposedly been turned over to LG to be addressed, but the South Korean consumer electronics conglomerate has plenty of other questions to answer here.
It’s finally happened: the improved quality of machine transcription and the greater ability to extract value from unlabelled data means “your tech is eavesdropping on you for marketing purposes” has crossed from “false conspiracy theory” to “true and concerning” www.theverge.com/tech/991190/…
— Alex Hern (@hern.bsky.social) 7:52 AM · Sep 8, 2026
Some of what the team found is already a fairly standard part of the shady business of serving personalized ads and recommendations on smart TVs, devices that many users tend to think of merely as 2000s-era televisions rather than the internet-equipped home computers (complete with apps) that they truly are. These various types of technology fall under the broader title of Automatic Content Recognition (ACR), which is the title for a suite of technologies used to monitor what the user is watching or browsing, and generally how they’re using the TV. Pretty much all smart TV manufacturers use various forms of ACR to do everything from log your viewing habits to scan the other devices you connect to the TV via HDMI ports. Many TVs theoretically allow you to turn these settings off, but it requires navigating through menus that 99.9% of users will never touch.
The LG smart TVs assessed by Gamers Nexus, meanwhile, took some of these ACR technologies to distressing new levels. The techs here recorded evidence that the TVs were scanning and probing other wi-fi enabled devices on the same network in order to build a more thorough customer profile of the user for advertisers, in order to determine things such as what smartphones or watches a user possessed. But presumably even worse in the eyes of the average user was the constant use of the TV’s built-in microphones to capture audio from the environment, even when the screen was powered down. In fact, not even disconnecting the TV from a wi-fi source stopped it from gathering audio data–it merely kept collecting and stored the data locally, to be sent once the internet access was restored.
This in particular would seem to fly directly in the face of LG’s previous statement that its televisions “do not collect, record, or store ambient conversations,” and that voice-recognition features in general must be first activated by the user. LG does not seem to have issued any more recent press statement on the sprawling video investigation put out in the last 24 hours by Gamers Nexus and its collaborators.
Oh good the LG TV spyware video dropped. youtu.be/6IFVTcM28KA
— Chris Person (@papapishu.bsky.social) 11:19 AM · Sep 7, 2026
If this somehow led to litigation against the company, however, there’s pretty recent precedent in the matter. Just a few months ago, Samsung settled a lawsuit with the office of the Attorney General of Texas, based on how its own smart TVs had been using ACR for data collection, monetization and serving advertisements. As part of that deal, Samsung was forced to agree to stop collecting ACR data from customers in Texas without them giving explicit consent for personal data collection. It does make one wonder if some other state will take notice of this investigation into LG TVs and conclude that its own residents have been wronged.
In the meantime, if you want to confirm whether your own smart TV is collecting data in order to shape the ads and content recommendations you see, each major manufacturer has its very own set of hoops for you to jump through. This piece provides a good walkthrough on how to disable ACR settings, if you wish, on TVs from most of the major manufacturers.
At the end of the day, it comes down to how much the user has already been effectively conditioned to give up any expectation of privacy, to the point that some will no doubt specifically want to keep such features active, because they genuinely want advertising that is informed by everything from their other devices, to their private conversations. To the rest of us, this is a deeply frightening prospect. Or as Gamers Nexus offered by way of comparison: “If you want Flock cameras on your living room wall, this is how you get Flock cameras on your living room wall.”

articles.summary:
A new investigation by Gamers Nexus reveals that certain LG smart TVs continue to collect user data and record ambient audio even when the devices are powered off.

### Key Points
- Researchers found that LG smart TVs use Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) to scan local Wi-Fi networks and identify connected devices like smartphones and watches.
- The investigation claims the TVs store audio data locally when disconnected from the internet, transmitting the information once a connection is restored.
- Security experts identified vulnerabilities in the TV software that could potentially allow hackers to exploit these data-gathering features.
- LG has not issued a formal response to the findings, which contradict the company's previous claims that it does not record ambient conversations.
- The report highlights that these data collection practices often remain active unless users manually navigate complex settings menus to disable them.

### Why it Matters
This investigation highlights the growing tension between consumer privacy and the aggressive data-harvesting practices embedded in modern internet-connected home appliances. The findings may trigger regulatory scrutiny similar to recent legal actions taken against other manufacturers regarding unauthorized data collection and advertising practices.

articles.title: People’s Picks: 4 Phone Brands Dominate, but 1 Reigns Supreme and It’s Not Apple
articles.author: Dashia Milden
articles.content:
Every few years, you may think about upgrading your smartphone. A lot of thought and research goes into your next choice, whether it’s the price, features or brand reputation. Maybe you’re eyeing the latest and greatest, or considering a different phone brand or model altogether. Our readers’ opinions may help you decide.
CNET’s People’s Picks dives into what our readers really think about their tech devices and services, like their internet service provider, TVs and even their mobile carrier.
This round was all about readers’ phone brands, just in time for Apple’s Sept. 9 Surprise and shine event, where we expect new iPhone models to be revealed. We asked about everything from brand loyalty to battery life, durability and even price-to-value. The results came down to four big-name tech brands. While there’s only one overall winner, other brands win in key categories that can make a big difference in your day-to-day tasks if you’re upgrading soon.
Overall winner: Google
Google is the overall winner for CNET’s People’s Picks for Phones. CNET averaged the scores across three categories to determine the overall satisfaction rating, which includes customer satisfaction, battery longevity and price-to-value.
Google wins with a score of 4.52 out of 5, while Motorola trails closely behind with 4.45.
“It’s no surprise to me that Google and Motorola scored top marks because both sell some of the most affordable phones that people can buy. Motorola’s Moto G series costs hundreds of dollars less than Apple’s cheapest iPhone,” said CNET’s Director of Content, Patrick Holland. “At $500, Google’s Pixel 10A is one of the best values that you can buy today, especially as phone prices spike due to the ongoing RAM shortage caused by AI and data centers. It just goes to show that in 2026, you can spend less than $500 and still have a great phone that lasts you years.”
On the other hand, Samsung and Apple trail behind with scores of 4.19 and 3.87, respectively. Both brands have evolved in the smartphone space with AI-powered features, upgraded cameras, and thinner phone designs, but fell short in this category.
“There are a few factors at play here, most notably that Google and Motorola ship a fraction of the phones that Samsung does — so Pixel and Razr buyers are a more devoted core of customers than the many who buy Galaxy phones,” said CNET Managing Editor of Mobile David Lumb. A Counterpoint Research report on phone shipments in the first quarter of 2026 noted that Google (3% of the US market) and Motorola (10%) combined accounted for half of Samsung’s market share (26%).
The other thing to remember is that Google sells mostly premium phones.
“Aside from the Pixel 10A as a midrange device. Motorola and Samsung have wider ranges of more affordable and cheap phones, so I’d guess there’s less consumer fondness at the lower end of the device price scale,” Lumb said.
Apple’s fourth-place spot is a tougher nut to crack. Perhaps consumers haven’t seen as many upgrades in successive years as they would like in new iPhones, or they’re miffed at the higher prices Apple’s phones sell for. What’s most likely the case, Lumb suggested, is that there are simply more people buying new iPhones. In the Counterpoint report above, Apple handsets accounted for 58% of all phones shipped in the US.
AI features
AI features like photo editing, live translation and AI-powered summaries are becoming the focal point for new smartphone models. But what matters more is how much you’ll use those built-in features. Google Pixel wins with 88% of its users saying their phone’s AI features are essential and occasionally useful.
“Out of the four brands, only one is a true AI company, and that’s Google. In fact, Google’s Gemini AI can run on phones from all four brands, including the iPhone via an app. The Gemini Assistant can be used on Motorola and Samsung phones,” said Holland.
Lumb added that Google has led the charge in both including and promoting AI features in its Pixel phones that people actually use, like Magic Eraser and live translation.
“Pixel owners have been using AI features for years, and combined with Google aggressively inserting its Gemini assistant throughout the phone, it makes sense that Samsung Galaxy owners would feel a lesser impact from AI.”
Samsung has made plenty of AI advancements, like a health assistant and browser upgrades, but it falls behind, with only 64% of its users saying the same. Apple and Motorola trail behind with 14% and 8% each. Most Motorola users say the phone lacked built-in tools or ignored them.
What few AI features are available on iPhones were introduced more recently, so it’s unsurprising that their owners wouldn’t consider them essential to daily use, Lumb said. While Gemini continues to evolve, Apple’s advanced AI Siri was delayed for years and will finally launch with the upcoming iOS 27. 
Battery life
Ties with Motorola 
For a phone’s battery to exceed expectations, it must last a day or more. Motorola and Google tie in this category, with 74% saying their phones’ batteries exceed expectations by lasting a full day or longer without needing to be charged. Comparatively, Samsung and Apple fall behind, with only about half (52%) saying their phones’ batteries exceed expectations, while others say they just meet expectations. Apple finishes last, with only 31% reporting the same for their iPhones’ batteries. Most said their phone needed to be charged midday. 
“The number one factor for battery life is how you use your phone. And I think this result speaks volumes about how much iPhone owners are on their phones,” said Holland.
CNET’s phone battery testing found that Apple’s phones had the longest battery life, with OnePlus placing second and Motorola third. However, the test doesn’t account for how you use your phone specifically each day – everyone is different. If you’re hyper-connected and your default is scrolling through social media apps or streaming videos, even the best battery life won’t be enough for you, Holland said. “Thankfully, Google, Motorola and Samsung, along with Apple, have all increased the charging speeds on their handsets to at least make topping them off less of a pain point.”
Motorola
Value
Motorola wins in price-to-value, with 82% of its readers saying it offers exceptional value by delivering more than its price suggests. Only 4% rate the brand as overpriced.
“Before Motorola brought back the Razr as a foldable phone, its most popular handsets were its Moto G line that start as low as $200 and top out at $350,” said Holland. “Motorola has deep, long-term relationships with phone carriers, which often sell these phones at a discount.”
Compared with other brands, 45% of Pixel owners say Google’s phone offers exceptional value, and 35% of Samsung users say the same.
The surprising fact is that Apple places fourth in this category, with 58% of iPhone users saying it’s overpriced. Only 12% find the phone’s value exceptional. However, many tech brands are raising prices due to the RAM shortage, which makes it tough to determine what’s worth the high cost.
“The only company that hasn’t raised prices on its phones this year is Apple. There’s a chance it might announce a price hike at its Sept. 9 event. The cheapest iPhone the company sells starts at $600. You can find incredible Android phones for less, like the Google Pixel 10A for $500,” said Holland.
Apple
Durability
Choosing a phone that doesn’t shatter, crack or leave you with a broken camera can make a big difference when you need one to last a few years. Some phones are more durable than others. Apple wins this category with 78% of readers saying it’s highly durable against drops and daily use with minimal to no damage. The remaining 22% either deal with normal wear and minor scuffs over time, report their phone as fragile or always have a heavy-duty case to protect it.
Holland said that when Apple released the iPhone 12 in 2020, it was the first to have a flat, dense build with squared-off sides to increase durability. In the years following, Samsung followed suit, adopting a flat build for its Galaxy S and S Plus models, and Google implemented a similar design with its Pixel phones.
Google follows closely behind with 72% saying their Pixel smartphone is highly durable, while 28% say it’s moderately durable.
Not as many readers with a Motorola say the phone is highly durable (65%), but even fewer readers with a Samsung (58%) phone say the same. Samsung users say their foldable phone and screens are fragile and only moderately durable. Some readers criticize the brand for the phone’s fragility and susceptibility to damage from drops.
Brand retention and loyalty
Despite Apple falling short in several categories, 86% of Apple users said they’re extremely likely to buy the same brand next time.
“Apple’s most popular product is the iPhone, but its iPhone-only features like iMessage and FaceTime, not found on Android, that keep people tied in,” said Holland. “Also, if you want to learn about how to use your iPhone or get it fixed, you can go to the Apple Store and talk with an actual human – I think those retail stores are Apple’s secret weapon.”
Whereas 79% of Samsung owners share the same sentiment for the brand. Over half of Google Pixel owners (58%) would buy a Google phone again, but only 42% of people with Motorola phones would. Other Motorola owners are using competitor research to determine their next phone purchase.
Methodology
CNET commissioned Alchemer to conduct the People’s Picks survey to compile data. The survey was carried out online, and all figures are from Alchemer. The total sample comprised 1,107 adults. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 plus). Fieldwork was undertaken from July 1 to July 28, 2026.
articles.summary:
Google has been named the overall winner in CNET’s 2026 People’s Picks for smartphones, outperforming Motorola, Samsung, and Apple in key categories like customer satisfaction and battery longevity.

### Key Points
- Google secured the top spot with a 4.52 out of 5 satisfaction rating, followed by Motorola at 4.45.
- Motorola ranked highest for price-to-value, with 82% of users reporting exceptional value for their devices.
- Apple led the durability category, with 78% of users praising the iPhone's resistance to drops and daily wear.
- Google Pixel users reported the highest engagement with AI features, with 88% finding them essential or useful.
- Apple maintains the highest brand loyalty, as 86% of iPhone owners stated they are extremely likely to purchase the brand again.
- The survey, conducted by Alchemer, gathered data from 1,107 U.S. adults between July 1 and July 28, 2026.

### Why it Matters
These results highlight a growing consumer preference for affordable, high-value devices over premium-priced handsets in a market impacted by rising hardware costs. While Apple retains strong brand loyalty through its ecosystem, the data suggests that competitors are successfully capturing market share by delivering superior battery performance and practical AI integration.

articles.title: Mathspace breach exposes data on over a million students and parents
articles.author: Sinisa Markovic
articles.content:
Mathspace breach exposes data on over a million students and parents
Mathspace has confirmed that attackers broke into its internal reporting system through an unpatched Metabase vulnerability and stole data belonging to more than a million students, parents, and school staff.
The Sydney-based maths education company wrote in a blog post that the vulnerability, in its self-hosted installation of Metabase, allowed attackers to obtain administrator access to the system without a legitimate login.
Metabase is a business intelligence tool used to connect to and explore company databases. It’s available as a free open-source, self-hosted version, or as a paid service with cloud and self-hosted options.
“On 3 September 2026, we confirmed that unauthorised parties had accessed an internal reporting system used by Mathspace and downloaded information on students, their parents or guardians, and school staff,” said Alvin Savoy CTO at Mathspace.
“Our investigation identified unauthorised access dating back to 10 August 2026, Australian Eastern Standard Time. We confirmed that information was downloaded from our Australian reporting database on 27 August,” added Savoy.
According to the company, the breach affected 1,079,819 people in total, all located in Australia and New Zealand.
The exposed data included usernames, first and last names, email addresses, country, time zone, user type, email-verification status, last-active date, last-login date, and date joined. Some of these are internal Mathspace identifiers tied to student accounts.
Mathspace said no academic records, assessment results, passwords, authentication tokens, or API credentials were exposed. The exposed data did not include records linking user accounts to their schools, though it said this may still be possible for schools with identifiable email domains.
“Customer passwords, single sign-on (SSO) tokens and other customer authentication credentials were not exposed,” Savoy noted.
“We have no evidence so far that the data has been published, distributed, sold or otherwise misused.”
Mathspace isn’t requiring a password reset, since login credentials weren’t exposed. It is warning, however, that the leaked names and email addresses could be used to make phishing attempts look convincing.
Savoy is advising users to be wary of unexpected messages, never share passwords or verification codes, and use a unique password for every account.
“Based on our investigation to date, you can continue using Mathspace for lessons and assignments. The affected internal reporting system has been taken offline,” Savoy concluded.
This is not an isolated case in which attackers used a vulnerability in Metabase to reach customer data. Framework, Tally, and Kilo Code all disclosed similar breaches in August 2026, after attackers exploited the same SQL injection flaw in their Metabase instances.
articles.summary:
Mathspace has confirmed a data breach affecting over one million users in Australia and New Zealand after attackers exploited an unpatched vulnerability in its internal reporting software.

### Key Points
- Attackers accessed the Mathspace reporting system between August 10 and August 27, 2026, by exploiting a known vulnerability in a self-hosted Metabase instance.
- The breach exposed the personal information of 1,079,819 students, parents, and school staff, including names, email addresses, and account activity timestamps.
- Mathspace stated that no passwords, academic records, or authentication tokens were compromised during the unauthorized access.
- The company has taken the affected reporting system offline and confirmed that no evidence currently suggests the stolen data has been sold or misused.
- Similar Metabase-related security incidents were reported by companies including Framework, Tally, and Kilo Code throughout August 2026.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the significant security risks associated with unpatched third-party business intelligence tools integrated into educational platforms. While sensitive academic records remain secure, the exposure of contact information increases the risk of targeted phishing attacks against students and their families.

articles.title: DLSS 5 proves that Nvidia has lost the plot
articles.author: Dipan Saha
articles.content:
DLSS 5 received an immensely negative reaction from players when it was first revealed in early 2026, and it seems Nvidia has not taken those complaints to heart. Instead, it doubled down, and the latest work-in-progress leaked build is a mixed bag.
While DLSS 5 looks genuinely good in certain select scenarios, it’s not what this is about. Nvidia’s slop filter introduces unnecessary detail and “realism”, which drastically alters the game beyond its intended look, and could set a dangerous precedent.
DLSS 5 destroys the original artistic vision of the game
Chasing realism isn’t what games are always about
DLSS 5 is not an upscaler. In fact, it actively alters the output and enhances it further, using generative AI to “render” a more photorealistic image. This makes it more computationally expensive compared to traditional DLSS, which kind of defeats the whole point of the tech, but I’m getting ahead of myself here…
And the results have been quite varied, to say the least. DLSS 5 seems to work best under older titles, bringing them to a modern “RTX remaster” equivalent. That is, until you look into the finer details.
DLSS 5 is way too strong of a filter, and much of the remastering done here is full of flaws, as you’d expect from any kind of AI-generated frame. Not to mention it looks downright terrible on many titles, with Final Fantasy VII Remake’s Cloud being the stuff of nightmares.
If anything, though, DLSS 5 ruins a game's graphical presentation. Games are designed with certain visual elements in mind, and forcibly applying a filter to change things so dramatically just doesn’t sit right with me.
Sure, you could argue that mods and reshade packs do the same thing, but Nvidia’s new shiny upscaler looks a lot worse in comparison. Not to mention, these community-driven shaders were created with intent — with each section of a game hand-crafted to suit the author’s tastes.
DLSS 5 in its current (beta) state is just a photorealism filter, and not all games aim for that. While Nvidia has confirmed that developers can fine-tune the DLSS 5 output to maintain the “original” artistic vision, it begs the question: why even ship games that need a visual filter to look as intended?
DLSS 5 has a massive impact on performance
And requires specific hardware to work
It’s not like DLSS 5 is a lightweight model either. Oh no, far from it — and the “upscaler” has been seen to slash frame rates by up to 50%, mandating the use of both traditional DLSS upscaling and frame generation to offset the difference, which works as well as you’d expect.
To make matters worse, it is also currently restricted to the RTX 5000 (Blackwell) Series, which means you’ll need a rather pricey GPU to even stand a chance at previewing this tech. You won’t be able to use this on something like an RTX 5060 well at all.
Nvidia plans to port it to the RTX 4000 Series later, although I wouldn’t be too optimistic about performance. Restricting the tech to current-gen cards that are mostly out of reach for most folks isn't a great outlook.
The so-called improvements on offer simply aren't worth the performance loss, and a broad majority will largely ignore them.
As the technology matures, it could slowly turn into a crutch
Another ray tracing-like situation could be on the horizon
I fear the worst with the eventual, full release of DLSS 5. The current crop of game tech, especially ray tracing and upscaling, has been a bane for gaming in recent years. While these were made with good intent, most games still overutilize them, to the point that they've become more of a crutch.
Running a modern AAA game at higher resolutions without upscaling often tanks frame rates below 60 FPS, making it mandatory no matter the card you use. The same can be said for ray tracing, which is being forced on every game these days.
DLSS 5 could pose a different kind of problem, though. By actively altering the game’s look, it could push developers to optimize for a DLSS 5 “exclusive” look, and because it would be gated behind specific GPUs, it would ultimately severely restrict the number of players who could achieve that “final” level of detail.
DLSS 5 is trying to solve a problem that does not exist
To address the elephant in the room, DLSS 5 is trying to solve a problem that doesn't exist. Just play games the way they were meant to look in the first place. This kind of implementation has absolutely zero reason to exist and is a slap in the face to most designers.
If anything, it could set off a wave of DLSS 5 “enhanced” titles that force the tech to be used. It really makes you think, though: Why not just design the game with the original look and intent (without relying on an AI filter to enhance things over), instead of producing generic, photorealistic abominations?
Until then, there’s not much to do but hope that AMD doesn’t follow suit, along with the rest of the industry.
articles.summary:
Nvidia’s upcoming DLSS 5 technology faces significant criticism for using generative AI to alter game aesthetics, causing performance drops of up to 50% on high-end Blackwell GPUs.

### Key Points
- DLSS 5 functions as a photorealism filter rather than a traditional upscaler, often overriding the original artistic intent of game developers.
- Early testing shows inconsistent visual quality, with reports of distorted character models and graphical artifacts in titles like Final Fantasy VII Remake.
- The technology is currently restricted to Nvidia’s RTX 5000-series graphics cards, with future support planned for the RTX 4000-series.
- Enabling the feature can reduce frame rates by as much as 50%, necessitating the simultaneous use of traditional upscaling and frame generation.
- Critics argue the tech acts as a performance-heavy crutch that may pressure developers to design games specifically for AI-enhanced visual outputs.

### Why it Matters
This technology represents a shift toward AI-driven visual modification that could fundamentally change how games are developed and experienced. If widely adopted, it risks creating a hardware-gated standard that prioritizes synthetic photorealism over the original creative vision of game designers.
